summary:
Manikyam, meaning "Hear the planet breathe", is an interactive Earth science sonification jukebox that we developed to explore how we can experience our planet beyond just seeing it. NASA provides incredible visualizations of Earth's changing climate and environment, but most of this information is presented visually, which can create accessibility barriers for blind and low-vision users.

With Manikyam, we wanted to create another way to experience this information through sound. The project uses scientific measurements and visual data extracted from video frames to generate musical soundscapes. Using computer vision, we extracted visual properties such as luminance and changes between frames, then map them to musical elements using Tone.js. The experience combines these sounds with interactive visualizations built using Pixi.js, allowing users to explore the relationship between data, visuals and audio.

We believe that Earth science should be experienced by everyone, not just through charts and images. Manikyam aims to make complex environmental patterns more approachable, accessible and emotionally engaging through a combination of science, technology and art.
details:
About the Project: Manikyam

Manikyam, meaning “Hear the planet breathe,” is an interactive Earth science sonification jukebox that explores a different way of experiencing our planet and its changing environment. Our idea is simple: instead of depending only on charts, graphs and visualizations to understand Earth science, what if we could also listen to the data?

Our project converts scientific datasets and visual information from Earth visualizations into sound. For example, monthly global temperature anomaly measurements can be mapped to musical elements such as pitch and intensity. For video-based visualizations, we use computer vision techniques to extract features such as luminance and changes between frames, which can then influence the generated sound. Users can listen to these soundscapes while exploring interactive visualizations, connecting what they see with what they hear.

Manikyam offers an alternative way to explore complex Earth science information. We aim to make environmental data more approachable, engaging and accessible, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. It can also help other users discover patterns in scientific data through sound.

We developed Manikyam using Python, Flask, NumPy and Pandas for data processing and the backend, JavaScript for the frontend, Tone.js for audio generation and PixiJS for interactive visualizations. We also use computer vision and video-processing techniques to extract information from visual data.

What makes Manikyam creative is the combination of science, music and interactive technology. Instead of simply presenting data in another visual format, we translate patterns into a sound experience. The musical mappings are interpretations of the data, not replacements for the original scientific measurements.

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, synchronization between audio and visuals, usability and performance. We also made sure to distinguish actual scientific measurements from features extracted from video, so users can understand what the sounds represent.

Our intended impact is to make Earth science something people can not only see and study, but also hear and experience. We believe understanding our planet should not depend only on the ability to interpret charts or see a visualization.
